summary: A CCC-built stone, wood and steel lookout on East Peak of Mount Tamalpais (completed 1936, named for Ed Gardner), still an active Marin County fire lookout.

facts.design: CCC-built sturdy stone, wood and steel tower on East Peak

staffing.status: active Marin County Fire Department lookout; volunteer-staffed in daytime (2014 report)

access.note: Active county fire lookout in Mount Tamalpais State Park; sources describe a view from the parking lot at the base of the peak and do not say the cab is open to visitors

visit.trail_note: Tower visible from the parking lot at the base of East Peak

events.note: NHLR gives 1934 as the built year; CCC Company 1920V worked on it between 1934 and 1936
New tower under construction by the CCC; to be named in honor of the late Fire Warden Ed Gardner
CCC completed the new tower by July 30, 1936; lookout moved into it and the old wooden building was set aside
Henry A. Long died in January 1940 after six years as Mount Tamalpais lookout; Fred Petri appointed in May 1940
Lookout spotted a San Anselmo fire that was hard to locate from the ground; about half an acre of grass burned

Four remote fire-detection cameras ($207,000 system, PG&E grant to FIRESafe Marin); two give 24-hour coverage on Mount Tamalpais and Mount Barnabe, where lookouts are daytime-only and volunteer-staffed
Registered September 21, 2015 as US 1115, CA 108; nominated by Don Keylon
Still actively used by the Marin County Fire Department as of 2019

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR gives 1934 as the built year and says the CCC worked there between 1934 and 1936. The state parks page says 1935 to 1936. A 1936 newspaper item says the CCC had completed the new tower by July 30, 1936. The story reports the NHLR range and the July 1936 completion.

A 1902 station built by William Randolph Hearst and earlier lookout buildings on Mount Tamalpais are different structures from the 1936 CCC tower. The sources do not say whether the wooden building replaced in 1936 was one of them, so the story does not link them.

notes_for_editor: The build date (1934 vs 1935-36) and the July 1936 completion are the main conflict; the story reports both. The brief's kind 'two_story' is not supported by any page read: NHLR and state parks describe a sturdy stone, wood and steel tower, and nothing read says it has two stories. Please check that field. The 1935-1940 history comes from newspaper clippings compiled by the Forest Lookouts site, cited as secondary. The 1950 'Ten Years Ago' weather-reading item is a 1940 retrospective and was left out. Search snippets not read: a Redwood Bark piece says 'Built in 1937', and an archive.org record says 'between 1935 and 1936'; a Marin County Fire history PDF mentions an earlier 1901 East Peak lookout station. None of those is in the story. The Living New Deal page was not read. The brief's vimeo and OpenStreetMap sources were not read. Visiting advice is limited to the parking-lot view; the sources do not describe public access to the cab.
